scores.evidence: Instagram is doing real work — 150 new customers a month (B3) is meaningful for a small e-commerce brand at this price point, and the brand has a website, two social profiles, and a video channel (A3, F1). But all meaningful discovery runs through one channel. Paid search has been tested and explicitly failed: (F3): "Google Shopping ads — £600 over two months, because in a thumbnail our £58 coat looks identical to the £14 one." A craft fair in Cirencester "sold two feeders" and a giveaway brought "900 followers who never bought a thing" (F3). No SEO or organic search strategy is mentioned anywhere in the intake — a significant gap given that rescue dog owners are actively searching for anxiety solutions, and Steady Hound has a genuine story to surface in those results.
scores.leak_cost_estimate: £300/mo in direct Google Shopping spend (explicitly £600 over 2 months, F3) producing no measurable return. Single-channel dependency risk: if Instagram shifts its algorithm, the current 150 new customers/month (B3) × £52 average sale (B2) = £7,800/mo in new-customer revenue is exposed with no fallback channel in place.

scores.evidence: When given enough room, the message is unusually clear. (A2): "We make calming kit for anxious dogs — a pressure coat, a den bed, slow feeders — all of it road-tested on a panel of genuinely nervous rescues before we'll sell a single one." That sentence covers who it is for, what it sells, and why it is different from a cheap Amazon coat in two sentences. The differentiation is further sharpened by (E3): "Every product goes through a trial panel of twelve genuinely anxious rescue dogs before launch, and we publish the fail rate — the feeder took three redesigns and we say so." The problem is format-dependence: this story needs space to breathe, and it collapses entirely in compressed environments — the Google Shopping thumbnail failure is a direct symptom of the premium justification disappearing at the point of the ad impression.
scores.leak_cost_estimate: Exact cost cannot be pinned to a single channel from the intake alone. As a floor: if just 2 of the 150 new customers per month (B3) are lost in any format-stripped channel because the rescue-panel story never appeared before they compared on price, that is 2 × £52 (B2) = £104/mo in missed first purchases — before accounting for the 60%+ who would have returned.

scores.evidence: There is a proven conversion asset in place: (F4): "the five-part introduction-guide email series — people who read all five emails buy the bundle at nearly triple the rate." That is the clearest evidence of a functioning path in the entire intake. The Instagram-to-first-purchase route is also working: (B4): "Reels of Bramble (my noise-phobic collie cross) doing settle training in her coat drive most first orders." What is missing is a clear on-site path for visitors who do not opt into the email series — no mention of a named bundle page, abandoned cart recovery, or a single obvious starting-point purchase for a new rescue dog owner discovering the brand. The best conversion mechanism available requires completing five emails before it does its work.
scores.leak_cost_estimate: No session or on-site conversion data was provided. Directionally: with 150 new customers/month (B3) at £52 average (B2), any visitor who arrives from Instagram, does not enter the email series, and compares on price alone is making a decision against Steady Hound. If 2 such visitors per month are lost, that is 2 × £52 = £104/mo — likely a conservative floor given the absence of a named bundle landing page.

scores.evidence: The email list is the most underperforming asset in the business. (F2): "About 2,400 subscribers. Last proper send was mid-June — a Bramble update plus the Den Bed restock. I aim for fortnightly and manage monthly, which needs fixing before October." The owner has already diagnosed the problem. The five-part welcome series (F4) is likely running as an automated sequence for new subscribers and is genuinely effective, but the broadcast newsletter — the channel that would re-engage the full 2,400 — has effectively stopped. No mention of abandoned cart sequences, post-purchase follow-up flows, or win-back campaigns for customers who have not ordered in 90-plus days. The 60%+ repeat rate (B6) is arriving via word of mouth and rescue Facebook groups, not managed email follow-up.
scores.leak_cost_estimate: If fortnightly sends reactivated just 4 existing subscribers per email (8 purchases/month), that recovers 8 × £52 (B2) = £416/mo at near-zero cost. Separately, mid-June to late October is approximately 8 missed planned broadcasts to 2,400 subscribers — all missed in the run-up to fireworks season, the highest-intent period for this exact product.

scores.evidence: The proof Steady Hound holds is genuinely unusual. (E3): "Every product goes through a trial panel of twelve genuinely anxious rescue dogs before launch, and we publish the fail rate — the feeder took three redesigns and we say so. Sizing videos for odd-shaped rescues, a handwritten intro guide in every box, and I answer the DMs myself." Publishing failure rates is rare; it signals confidence and builds trust that polished brand copy cannot manufacture. Bramble is living, ongoing proof on Instagram. The gap is placement: there is no mention of where customer reviews or testimonials live on the website, whether product pages show a review count, or whether the rescue-panel story appears in ad creative or at the top of product descriptions. The proof exists; it is unclear whether it sits where it does the most conversion work.
scores.leak_cost_estimate: No direct spend is being wasted on proof specifically. The hidden cost: if 2 shoppers per month land on a product page without seeing the rescue-panel story or a customer review count and buy elsewhere, that is 2 × £52 (B2) = £104/mo lost — and at a 60%+ repeat rate, those would likely have been returning customers too.

scores.evidence: The products are clearly working — (B6): "60%+" repeat customers means people come back, and (B4) shows a natural product progression: "repeat customers come back for the bed and the treat pouches." But the offer as packaged at the point of discovery is weak. (E2): "We also lose bundle sales to PawsRelax's £39 'starter set' when people shop on price alone." There is no named starter bundle to compete with or position against. The email series unlocks bundle conversion at nearly triple the rate (F4), but only after five emails. The premium positioning (E4) is stated but the offer architecture — individual product listings, no named kit, no visible entry point for a first-time rescue owner — does not currently make the premium feel inevitable.
scores.leak_cost_estimate: If 2 customers per month choose PawsRelax's £39 bundle over a non-existent Steady Hound starter bundle, that is 2 × £52 (B2) = £104/mo in lost first purchases. At a 60%+ repeat rate those customers would likely have returned: 2 lost customers/month × 12 months = 24 lost customers/yr × £52 × 2 orders each (initial plus one repeat) = £2,496/yr from just 2 missed first-time shoppers per month.

top_3_leaks: Dormant email list entering peak season: 2,400 opted-in subscribers have had one broadcast since mid-June (F2), and fireworks night — the single highest-intent buying period for nervous-dog products in the UK calendar — arrives in weeks. The five-part welcome series triples bundle conversion for new subscribers but does nothing for the existing 2,400 who have already cleared it or never received a follow-up broadcast.

Google Shopping spend producing no return: £300/month (£600 over 2 months, F3) is being spent in a channel where the £58 pressure coat is visually indistinguishable from a £14 Amazon lookalike in a small thumbnail — the brand's entire premium justification is stripped out at the exact moment of the ad impression, and no increase in budget can fix a format mismatch.

No packaged starter bundle on the website: the brand is explicitly losing sales to PawsRelax's £39 starter set (E2) while its own strongest conversion mechanism — the email bundle offer — is locked behind a five-email sequence. A new visitor arriving from a shared Reel has no obvious named kit to buy and no single page where the rescue-panel story and the product range sit together as a clear starting point.
quick_wins: Write and send one broadcast email to your 2,400 subscribers this week — open with a fireworks-season warning, include a recent photo of Bramble in the coat, and link directly to the pressure coat product page. It costs nothing, takes two hours to write, and lands at exactly the highest-intent moment in your entire year.

Pause all Google Shopping campaigns today and move that £300/month budget to boosting two or three existing Bramble Reels that have already driven first orders — stop funding the channel that shows your coat beside £14 lookalikes and put the money behind the channel where conversion is already happening.

Create a named starter bundle page on your website this week — combine the pressure coat and den bed under a single name such as 'The Settle Kit', open the page with the twelve-dog rescue-panel story and the three-redesign detail, price it clearly, and swap your Instagram bio link to point there instead of the homepage.
narrative_summary:
Steady Hound has something most small e-commerce brands spend years trying to build: a real character in Bramble, a story that is genuinely different from every competitor — publishing your failure rates takes confidence — and a repeat-purchase rate above 60%. Those are not vanity numbers. They mean people trust the product enough to come back and tell other rescue owners about it. Instagram is working, 150 new customers a month without meaningful paid support is a real result, and the five-part email series is one of the sharpest conversion tools I have seen described at this stage of a business.

The problems are fixable, and most share the same root: the best parts of this business — the rescue-panel story, the email series, the Bramble content — are not being deployed consistently across all the places customers land.

The most urgent issue is the email list. 2,400 people signed up to hear from you, and they have had one email since June. That is weeks before fireworks night, which for an anxious-dog brand is the equivalent of a retailer going silent in mid-November. Send something this week — it will cost you two hours and nothing else.

The Google Shopping spend is simply wasted. The thumbnail format removes every reason someone should pay £58 over £14. No amount of budget fixes a format mismatch — pull it now and redirect the money to Reels, where conversion is already proven.

The structural fix that will compound is a named starter bundle. Your email series sells the bundle beautifully, but it takes five emails to do it. A first-time visitor from Instagram needs a page that does the same job in ninety seconds.
